newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Upstart Smart surpasses Philippine telecom firms.
newsitem.headline: Upstart Smart surpasses Philippine telecom firms.

text.p: After successfully challenging entrenched players in the Philippine cellular telephone industry, upstart Smart Communications Inc has set its sights on lucrative international telecom and multi-media services.

"Smart will be a premier integrated telecom company by then ... We intend to be the service provider of choice," Smart president and chief executive officer Orlando Vea told Reuters when asked how he saw Smart in five years time.

The domestic telecommunications industry has been and still is dominated by the Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co (PLDT). Its strength was born during the long reign of former strongman Ferdinand Marcos who divided the country's vital industries among selected oligarchs.

Vea, together with his partners, decided to crack open the monolithic and inefficient industry, applying for a congressional franchise in 1991 even before the government decided to liberalise the industry in 1993.

As a result, Smart was the first one to be given a cellular mobile telephone service licence under the liberalised regime, attracting Hong Kong's First Pacific Co Ltd and its subsidiary Metro Pacific Corp to invest in the firm.

"The mobile service we thought presented the best opportunity for entry ... We thought mobile phones could serve both the mobile requirement as well as serve as an alternative to the land line," Vea said.

Smart launched an aggressive marketing tack by offering low- priced packages for cellular telephones which were being marketed as an upscale and high-technology product by its competitors, Pilipino Telephone Corp, a subsidiary of PLDT, and Express Telecommunication Co Inc.
"We deliberately chose a technology that was then matured in terms of technical application and economies of scale, which means that we could get our handsets at a lower price," Vea said.
Smart offered their phones to corporate executives as well as their sons and daughters. Subscribers grew by 25,000 to 30,000 every month.
After three years in full operation, Smart has wrested the number one spot from Piltel in terms of subscriber base. By February, it had 362,000 subscribers against Piltel's 357,000.
Vea said Smart was not hit by cloning and subscription fraud which severely affected its competitors, because it was able to set up controls on its technology and collection system.
With the success in the mobile segment, Smart is now venturing into other sectors of the thriving industry.
Smart recently bought a 9.8 percent stake in Eastern Telecommunications Phils Inc, a subsidiary of Cable & Wireless Plc, and is expected to bring it up to 49.8 percent soon.
"Eastern is very strong on corporate international services. With our acquisition, it will present a good coverage of the market," Vea added.
Smart had rolled out 161,000 land lines by end of 1996 and these are expected to reach 391,000 by the end of this year.
Smart has also set up a joint venture company with Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, one of its major shareholders, to offer multimedia services in the country.
UBS Securities (East Asia) Ltd analyst Richard Moe, in a report, said Smart "is well positioned to triple its profits in 1997." Last year, Smart reported a 254 million peso net income.
Smart is set to offer 450 million of its common shares by June or July this year with the price ranging from 12 pesos (45 cents) to 20 pesos (76 cents) per share.
The initial public offering is one of the much awaited issues set to come out this year, Patrick Carague, an analyst at DBP-Daiwa Securities (Phils) Inc, said.
(Conversion: $1 = 26.30 pesos)
